inline.s: In the Ming dynasty, Zheng Lian of Pujiang had a household whose members, for two hundred years, never left their ancestral home to move elsewhere. Everyone called the village where he lived the “Righteous Gate.” The prefect of the time sent a plaque praising his family that read: “The First Story of All Under Heaven.” After the founding emperor Taizu of the Ming ascended the throne, he summoned Zheng Lian to the capital and asked him: “When your household begins to cook, how many people sit down to eat?” Zheng Lian replied: “A little over a thousand.” The emperor said: “Truly it is the first story under heaven!” At the time Empress Ma was listening behind a folding screen, and she said to the emperor: “Your Majesty obtained the realm by rising up as a single person; now Zheng Lian’s household actually numbers over a thousand. If they were to rise up, would it not be all the easier for them to take the realm?” Hearing these words, the emperor was genuinely startled, and asked Zheng Lian again: “What method do you use to keep your kinsmen dwelling together in harmony?” Zheng Lian answered with great cleverness: “I have no other method except that I simply do not listen to my wife’s words!” The emperor could not help laughing out loud. At the time Henan happened to present fragrant pears to the court, and the emperor therefore bestowed two pears upon Zheng Lian. Zheng Lian raised the pears above his head with both hands and walked out of the palace, whereupon the emperor had someone follow and watch him. After Zheng Lian returned home, he gathered his kinsmen, bowed his head to the ground toward the direction of the imperial palace to return thanks, and in two large vats of water crushed the pears and placed them in the vats, so that every person of the whole clan tasted the pears bestowed by the emperor. When the emperor heard of this, he was greatly pleased. Later, someone exposed the Zheng family, claiming they had colluded with a powerful minister to rebel. The emperor said: “There is no such person in the Zheng family; it is others who have falsely accused them!” Afterwards the emperor issued an edict ordering the Zheng family to select sons and younger brothers over thirty years of age to come to the capital, and the court conferred office upon them. The clan elder Zheng Ying came to the palace to return thanks, and the emperor himself came to the Fengtian gate, wrote the three characters “Filial and Righteous Family” with his own brush and bestowed them, and even affixed the imperial seal upon them!
A man who is not loyal, sincere, and good.

To exhaust oneself is called loyalty; to be upright and correct is called goodness. Man is the most intelligent of all beings, and among humans the man is honored. Since one has attained this body of a man, honored and intelligent, and yet is crafty and disloyal, unable to fulfill his own duty, and is wicked and unrighteous, unable to be an upright person — then he has not only betrayed his own intelligence, but has betrayed Heaven above as well!

The Song-dynasty Lord Wen Zheng Gong (Fan Zhongyan) lost his father at the age of two. When he grew older he stood on his own, and studied day and night, sitting in stillness and contemplating in silence. After six years of this he mastered the Six Classics. At the age of twenty he passed the imperial examination and served as the prefect of Hezhong. He was just and upright in office, governed his household with order, and knew well how to use both kindness and authority. In bestowing alms to relieve the poor and rescue the suffering, he spared no effort. For this reason Fan Zhongyan not only gained a great name for a time, but was also honored and revered by a hundred generations. So the word “man” may truly be said to be one that Mr. Fan was fully worthy of!
A woman who is not gentle and obedient.

The Record of Rites says: “The man leads, the woman follows.” It says again: “When a woman is young, she follows her father and elder brothers; after she is married, she follows her husband; after her husband dies, she follows her son.” The Family Instructions of Master Yan says: “The duty of a woman is only to preside over the proper usages of food, dress, and adornment in the household. If a woman possesses intelligence and talent, she should only assist her husband and make up for his shortcomings. If she places herself above her husband and meddles in outside affairs, she is like the hen that crows at dawn, or the long-tongued and garrulous owl. That the family fortune does not prosper has its beginning right here!”

The Lady Hou, wife of the Song-dynasty Cheng Xiang, was exceedingly humble and gentle. Even for the smallest matter she would report to her husband before acting. She governed her household well and never beat or scolded the servants. When her children reproved the servants, she would surely admonish them, saying: “Although people differ in high and low station, their personhood is equally honorable!” When her husband Cheng Xiang was angry, she would always gently advise him at his side, so that he could let go his wrath and his mood improve. Only when the children erred would she not cover for them. She often said: “The reason children turn out unworthy is that the mother protects and covers for them, so that the father never learns of the children’s faults!” Later her two sons, Cheng Yi and Cheng Hao, both became famous Confucian scholars of the Song dynasty, and their status was most exalted. Even after death they enjoyed the honor of having offerings placed for them in the Confucian temple.

The Zixia Formula for Building Fortune says: “For a woman who cultivates virtue, it is no different from a man. But a woman has no other business; if she can accomplish the three obediences and four virtues, only then is she a good woman. If there is a good deed, it is better to urge one’s parents and husband to do it. Therefore, if parents do three good deeds, the woman shares in one; if the husband does two, the wife shares in one. If it is brought about by the wife’s forethought and persuasion, then it is the same merit as the husband’s. If one can persuade a woman to do good, this merit is more precious than the woman doing good herself. Among sisters and sisters-in-law, if there is a good deed, they should praise one another; this merit is also equal. The most important thing is to rejoice in one’s heart and do good together, and not give rise to envy! If a woman can attain filialty and obedience, and assist her husband and teach her children, fulfilling her own duty, and moreover deeply believe in cause and effect, eat vegetarian food and recite the Buddha’s name, then in this present life she will naturally be at peace in body and mind, with flourishing descendants; and at death she will surely receive the compassionate guidance of the Buddha and be reborn in the Western Land. Therefore a woman should only cultivate quietly at home and should not rush about outside. In this way she will not waste her precious time, and may also avoid causing others to criticize her. Again, for example, if a child of the household is ill, and one prays to the spirits and performs offerings for protection, it easily costs a good deal of money. Why not instead, at ordinary times, do good deeds and release living creatures? Then one will naturally receive the protection of the spirits. Thus, within the inner quarters one can naturally cultivate virtue and build blessings. I hope that all women will encourage one another and strive to do this!”
Husband and wife who are not in harmony.

The common saying goes: “A harmonious household makes all things prosper.” The ancients said: “Only when husband and wife are in harmony is the family way prosperous.” If a woman has never studied and understood principle, and does something wrong, the husband should clearly explain and guide her. Certainly he should not indulge her, nor should he immediately become angry and resentful. But if a husband meets a fierce and shrewish wife, he will be subjected to her bullying; and if he meets a weak and simple wife, he instead humiliates and mistreats her. To bully the weak and fear the strong — is this what a husband should do? All the more there are foolish husbands who dote on a concubine and insult the primary wife, or who are infatuated with a courtesan and mistreat their wife, and even beat and rage at her. Such husbands especially do not come to a good end!

Gu Kai treated his wife with great propriety. He often went out early and returned late, so his wife seldom saw his face. Once, when Gu Kai was gravely ill and lying in bed, his wife came out to see him. Gu Kai ordered those at his side to help him up, and put on his cap and cloak, then exchanged greetings with his wife, and only after the ritual was completed did he tell his wife to return to her room.

From this we may see that between husband and wife, how can there be even a single moment without propriety? If husband and wife can treat each other with propriety, how could they ever fall out of harmony? Yet is it difficult to observe propriety? One only needs to be harmonious yet restrained, and loving yet respectful, and that is enough!

Wang Balang of Luoyang had a cruel temper and loved to beat his wife. He was infatuated with a courtesan and had nearly squandered his family fortune. His wife was already suffering hunger and cold, yet Wang Balang beat her all the more severely. His wife, having no recourse, could only entrust relatives and neighbors to help settle the matter. Wang Balang then ordered his wife to move elsewhere and lived with the courtesan in the same room. Not long after, Wang Balang fell gravely ill, and his property was already exhausted. At that point the courtesan drifted away on her own. Having no way out, Wang Balang then wished to take refuge with his wife again, but by then she avoided him. Suddenly Wang Balang died of an abrupt illness, and soon after his wife died too. The relatives and neighbors could only place the two corpses together. That night, they suddenly heard sounds of fighting and quarreling inside the house. When they opened the door and looked, the bodies of the couple Wang Balang were standing back to back.
A wife who does not respect her husband.

The ancients said: “The husband is the wife’s heaven.” The husband is the person a wife relies on for her whole life. So how could a wife fail to respect her husband? A wife who does not respect her husband is either a shrew or a wanton woman: either she contradicts her husband with harsh words, or she curses him. Yet she does not know that whoever is reborn as a woman, it is mostly because in past lives she created evil karma. If she again bullies her husband, in her next life she will fall into the three evil paths! As for a woman who, when her husband has just died and his bones are not yet cold, already wishes to remarry, who regards the children she bore her husband as strangers, and who does not even grieve at her husband’s death — when her husband was alive, how could she have respected him at all?

Du Qi was by nature extremely timid and weak. His wife, Lady Zhang, had always looked down on him. In his later years he was often ill, and his wife neither attended to him nor took care of him. Strangely enough, Lady Zhang died before Du Qi. After Lady Zhang was placed in her coffin, the coffin suddenly broke open, and Lady Zhang was transformed into a python that rushed straight into the forest.
Alas! The ancients said: “The husband is the wife’s heaven.” So to slight one’s husband is the same as slighting Heaven! Can Heaven be slighted? Let all who are wives think carefully on this!

In the Later Han dynasty, Liang Hong took the daughter of the Meng family as his wife. Meng Guang, when she married into the Liang household, was dressed in gold and silver and adorned most elegantly and luxuriously. After seven days had passed, Liang Hong would not speak a single word to her. So Meng Guang gathered up her hair, pinned it on top of her head, changed into plain clothing of coarse cloth, and set about the household chores. Only then did Liang Hong say with joy: “This is truly Liang Hong’s wife!” Thereupon he went with his wife into seclusion in the Baling mountains. Later, to avoid troubles, he went to the state of Wu and lodged in a small hut beside the residence of Gao Botong, where he was hired to husk rice. Every time Liang Hong returned home after work, his wife had already prepared his meal and set it before him, and she did not dare to lift her head to look up, her manner most respectful. Gao Botong, seeing how Liang Hong’s wife raised the tray (bowl) level with her eyebrows in serving her husband, said: “Liang Hong here is only a worker who husks rice, and yet he can make his wife serve him with such respect. He is surely no ordinary person!” So he invited the couple Liang Hong to move into his home.

There is no greater way for a wife to respect her husband than in these two matters: preserving her chastity for her husband, and being skilled at teaching her children. As the saying goes, “A virtuous woman does not serve two husbands.” When a widow preserves her chastity for her husband, even ghosts and spirits will respect her. For example, in the Ming dynasty the academician Huang Guan died for the state during the disaster of the Jingkang era. His wife, Lady Weng, and his two daughters were captured. To avoid the humiliation of herself and her daughters, Lady Weng seized the moment and took her daughters to drown themselves. Her act of preserving her chastity for her husband is revered by a thousand ages; and so to this day, in the temple by the Qinhuai River, Lady Weng’s memorial tablet is still enshrined. And in the Song dynasty, the father of Ouyang Xiu died when Ouyang Xiu was four. His mother, Lady Zheng, preserved her widowhood for her husband. Their life was very poor; besides working to earn money to support the family, she had personally to teach Ouyang Xiu to write and to read, enduring all hardship and bitterness. This so moved Ouyang Xiu to strive in his studies that he finally became a wise and worthy prime minister of the Song dynasty. Lady Zheng was also repeatedly granted by the court the titles of Grand Lady of Yue and Grand Lady of Wei. These two cases are models of respecting the husband, and all who are wives should take them as their own encouragement!
One who often delights in pride and self-conceit.

Laozi said: “He who does not think himself right makes his thought stand out; he who does not praise himself has his merit affirmed; he who is not proud is able to sustain the growth of his undertaking.” The Book of Changes says: “The way of Heaven, whatever it be: whoever is proud and self-satisfied it causes to lose, and the humble it lets gain benefit. The way of earth, whatever it be: whoever is proud and self-satisfied it causes to change, not letting him be forever satisfied, and the humble it lets be moistened and never dried, just as where a low place is, the flowing water passing by surely fills its defect. The way of ghosts and spirits: whoever is proud it causes to be harmed, and the humble it lets receive blessing. If one is high and noble yet humble, his virtue is all the more radiant; if one is low and humble yet humble, his virtue also cannot be surpassed. Therefore humility is a virtue the gentleman always preserves!” Great Yu was not proud and did not praise himself, and said: “Even the foolish man and woman have strengths in which they surpass me!” So Great Yu, not proud and not self-praising, was finally able to overcome a myriad difficulties, dredge the rivers, and tame the great flood, so that his merit extended to a myriad ages. And the Duke of Zhou, whose talent overshadowed the age, not only was not proud and not stingy, but was also exceedingly humble, respectful, diligent in government, and loving to the people, and finally completed the great enterprise of unifying the Eastern Expedition, laying for the Zhou dynasty a foundation of lasting peace. So it is said that the truly great sages and worthy men are all made bit by bit from a place of trembling caution, as if treading upon deep ice and facing a precipice! Great Yu and the Duke of Zhou were both sages; when did they ever parade their own virtue before others? Yet now people casually take pride and boast before others, not knowing what the point is. In fact, others merely see in them nothing more than the self-importance of the man of Yelang!

In the Han dynasty, Gu Yong had been enfeoffed as a marquis for three days, yet his family did not know of it. In the Jin dynasty, Xie An was playing chess with a guest, and the report of victory at the Battle of Fei River arrived, yet the guest did not notice. The Song-dynasty general Cao Bin, when he conquered Jiangnan and returned to the capital to be received by the emperor, in the memorial submitted at the gate just said: “Returning after handling official matters in Jiangnan by imperial command.” The Song-dynasty worthy minister Wen Yanbo, during the Zhihe era of Emperor Renzong of Song, was the first to propose establishing Yingzong as crown prince (Yingzong reigned four years). When Emperor Shenzong later ascended the throne, Wen Yanbo said it was entirely Han Qi’s merit. The emperor thereby knew that Wen Yanbo did not boast of his own merit. These worthies named above are all of first-rate character, and their contribution to the state was very great. They were still able to be so retiring and not proud. Why do people not realize they should emulate them?

A person of great capacity surely has thick fortune; a person of shallow capacity surely has thin fortune. And humility and pride are the very boundary between calamity and blessing, so how can one be careless? Moreover, what is there in wealth, nobility, and ability sufficient to be relied upon? If one uses them to be arrogant before others, let alone whether calamity will come on account of it — first of all one has already lost one’s own heart and knows no shame!

In the Jin dynasty, Shi Chong and Wang Kai vied in ostentatious display of wealth, seeing who was richer. Wang Kai made a purple-silk screen wall forty li long, and Shi Chong made a brocade screen wall fifty li long, precisely to outdo Wang Kai. Wang Kai once brought out a coral a foot long given to him by the emperor to flaunt before Shi Chong. Shi Chong picked up an iron ruyi and smashed the coral, whereupon Wang Kai flew into a great rage. Shi Chong then brought out corals treasured in his own home, all two or three feet tall, and offered one to Wang Kai in compensation. As for the other rare and precious objects, the two kept striving to see whose were better. Later, when Shi Chong, because of a crime, was about to be beheaded, he sighed and said: “Is not your purpose in killing me to get my family property!”

Alas! The words Shi Chong spoke just before he died were so wise! But if he had known earlier, surely he would not have boasted! And the calamity of pride and self-conceit is just this cruel. So in every word and act of ours, how can we fail to be careful and cautious?
One who often contends for favor and is envious.

Both men and women have hearts of envy. A man who sees another achieving fame is jealous; when he sees another wealthy and noble, he is jealous; when another’s position draws near to his own, he is jealous; when another’s ability surpasses his, he is jealous. All these come from the narrowness of his own mind! As for a woman who, to contend for favor, forms resentments, she often brings calamity upon the household, and may even cut off the line of descendants — this sin is all the more grave. To such a degree that while alive everyone gnashes their teeth at her in hatred, and after death she sinks forever into the three evil paths of hell, hungry ghosts, and beasts, to repay the wicked debts she has created. So to rectify the mind and cultivate the person, and to be a model for others — is that the responsibility of men alone?

In the Zhou dynasty, General Pang Juan of the state of Wei, out of envy of Sun Bin’s talent, had Sun Bin’s two feet cut off; later he was killed by Sun Bin. In the Tang dynasty, the eunuchs Yu Chaoen and Cheng Yuanzhen envied Guo Ziyi’s high merit and great office. Every time they wished to slander and harm Guo Ziyi, in the end they instead were both convicted; Yu Chaoen was executed, and Cheng Yuanzhen was demoted and banished to a distant place. The Song-dynasty treacherous minister Han Tuozhou envied Zhu Xi’s promotion to the post of acting grand secretary at the Huanzhang Pavilion, and therefore formed a faction to denounce Zhu Xi’s learning as false. For a time the gentlemanly men were all cast out and suppressed; later Han Tuozhou was killed by Shi Miyuan. In the Northern Qi dynasty, the monk Mingchen, whenever he saw anyone more accomplished than himself, would envy him greatly; later Mingchen in the forest was transformed into a python and crawled off into a mountain valley. And when Emperor Wu of Liang obtained a formula for stopping envy, one beside him said to Emperor Wu: “I wish Your Majesty would widely bestow this formula for stopping envy upon the assembled ministers, so that those without ability would not envy the able; those harboring selfishness would not envy the selfless; those not pure would not envy the pure; those covetous of wealth would not envy the incorruptible. This too is a means of reforming them.” Emperor Wu gladly agreed. From these historical cases, we see that the affliction of envy is not only among women; men too are subject to it!

In the Zhou dynasty, the wife of Su Bao of the state of Song was named Nüzong. She served her mother-in-law with great filialty, while Su Bao held office in the state of Wei, where he served for three years and there took another wife. Su Bao’s elder brother’s wife then told this news to Nüzong. Nüzong said: “For a wife to serve her husband, it is single-minded devotion that is chastity and good compliance that is obedience; it is not established as virtuous to monopolize the husband’s love! According to the rules of propriety, a senior minister may take three wives and a knight may take two wives. My husband is a knight, so is it not a good thing for him to have two wives? Moreover, a woman has the seven grounds of dismissal (the seven conditions by which a man in ancient times divorced his wife), and envy is the first condition for a wife to be dismissed by her husband! Instead of telling me the proper way of the inner chambers for a wife, you would make me envious and cause me to commit the act of being dismissed by my husband?” The ruler of Song heard of this and issued an order to honor her, calling her Nüzong, to serve as a model for women.

Lu Bian’s uncle served as the magistrate of Hucheng county, and Lu Bian went to Hucheng to visit him. When he slept at night he had a dream in which he came to a place where there were ten large millstones, and beside the millstones were countless women. The millstones kept turning without stopping, and ox-headed ghost soldiers scooped up the women with large dustpans and threw them into the holes of the millstones. The women’s bodies then turned and were ground with the millstones, their flesh and bones all crushed to powder, their cries of pain unbearable to hear. Lu Bian saw his aunt among them too; when the two met, they felt both grief and joy. Lu Bian asked his aunt the reason for her suffering here. His aunt said: “This is all because in my former life I was envious; after death I have come here to suffer!” Alas! The hellish retribution of envy is indeed this dreadful!

In the Jin dynasty, the wife of Jia Chong, Lady Guo, was naturally prone to envy. She once bore a son. One day, the wet nurse was just holding the son, and Jia Chong took the opportunity to make improper advances to the wet nurse. Just then his wife came upon them. Lady Guo beat the wet nurse to death with a whip. The son, missing the wet nurse, cried himself to death, and Jia Chong thereby lost all descendants.

Jia Chong was a great treacherous minister who misled the state, so Heaven caused him to marry an envious wife in order to cut off his posterity. Yet the number of people in the world who, because of envy, suffer the retribution of being cut off from descendants is by no means small! And these envious women, even if they do not know how grave their sin is and that after death they cannot escape the retribution of hell, should at least fear the retribution of losing children before their eyes, the pain of the separation of flesh and bone, and the desolation of having no one to make offerings to them afterwards. So all women should early consider how severe and dreadful the retribution of envy is, and naturally they will no longer dare to be envious. If we carefully examine the case of Jia Chong, the retribution of being cut off from descendants was originally ordained by Heaven; and that he should happen to marry the envious Lady Guo as his wife is itself an ingenious form of evil retribution. So how can men fail to think of accumulating virtue to turn back Heaven’s intent, and only blame the envy of women?

In the Later Wei dynasty, the wife of Du Chang, Lady Liu, was very envious. One time, after Du Chang had washed his hair, he called the maidservant Jin Jing to comb it. When Lady Liu saw this she flew into a rage and cut off Jin Jing’s fingers. Not long after, Lady Liu was bitten by a fox, and the fingers of both her hands thus dropped off. There was another maidservant named Yulian who sang very well, and Du Chang was very fond of her. Lady Liu cut out Yulian’s tongue, so that she could no longer sing. Later Lady Liu’s tongue grew sores and rotted, and her condition was most critical. She went to the Chan master Chou to confess. The master said: “My lady, you cut off the maidservant’s fingers, and your own fingers have accordingly dropped off; again you cut out the maidservant’s tongue, and now your tongue is about to be cut off as well. Therefore you must repent with utmost sincerity before this disaster can be removed!” Lady Liu bowed to the master and begged earnestly. After seven days, the master made Lady Liu open her mouth wide, and then recited a spell toward Lady Liu’s mouth. At this, two snakes slowly crawled out more than a foot from Lady Liu’s mouth. The master recited the spell all the more urgently, and then the snakes fell to the ground. Lady Liu’s tongue thereby recovered, and from then on she was never envious again.

Therefore, when one repents of one’s faults and mends one’s evil ways, both spirits and humans rejoice. Even if one has committed boundless evil karma, so long as from now on one repents and does not repeat it, the sins committed before can be immediately melted away.
[Conclusion]

The common saying goes: “A woman’s resentment is not easily ended; a woman’s temper also readily forms resentments with others.” So cruel, venomous, and treacherous things, a woman will do with her own hands and not feel a moment’s doubt! Only when a woman is not yet married should her parents and brothers instruct her in advance; and once she is married, one should tactfully restrain her, and not fan the flames of her temper. In this way her heart of envy may be somewhat diminished. And the duty of mediating and transforming her falls upon her husband. If the husband, greedy for female beauty and fond of licentiousness, causes his wife to roar like a lioness, then the gentleman lays the guilt of the debauched husband upon his head — and this is still to be counted especially light!
A husband who treats his wife unrighteously and unkindly.

In treating one’s wife, one should be gentle and respectful; in treating one’s children, one should be strict and upright. If one cannot treat one’s wife with propriety, one loses the righteousness of the husband leading and the wife following. If one cannot use principle to teach one’s children, one harms the kindness of a father in begetting and raising children. To be unrighteous and unkind is called being without proper conduct. Today many who are husbands, in treating their wives, are either harsh and ungrateful or irreverent and indecorous; in treating their children, they are either over-indulgent or over-severe. They themselves are already unrighteous and unkind — how then can they go and blame their wives?

In the Later Han dynasty, Zhang Zhan was by nature grave and dignified, and exceedingly fond of propriety. He often explained the principles of conducting oneself in the world to his wife and children, just as a ruler leads his ministers. So his wife too was able to encourage and urge herself and him, and they urged each other on mutually. Hence he had considerable reputation in his home district. Zhang Zhan’s example may serve as a model for teaching wife and children.

Shi Tang married his wife at a very young age. Later, when he passed the examination and attained rank, he often regretted that he had not been able to marry the daughter of a wealthy family, and so felt great remorse. He then stopped paying attention to his wife and no longer shared the room with her. Because of this his wife grew depressed and downcast; as time passed she fell ill, and the illness continued for several years. Shi Tang never once looked in on her. His wife thus felt great anguish. When she was about to die, she called out to Shi Tang from the next room: “I am about to die. Can you really bear not to see me one last time?” Shi Tang was hard-hearted enough not to see his wife even that last time. A year after his wife died, the underworld authorities, because Shi Tang had treated his wife harshly and ungratefully, without feeling or righteousness, stripped away his lifespan and fortune, and Shi Tang suddenly died of illness.

Wang Yao of Zhuozhou doted excessively on his two sons, and so fostered evil dispositions in them. He himself could not control his sons and had to take them to the authorities. Later both sons died, and Wang Yao was thus left without posterity. After Wang Yao died, on the night of the fifteenth day of the second month of the following year, Liu Jin, the shrine keeper of the City God temple of Zhuozhou, saw a man holding a petition requesting from the City God an offering at the Qingming festival. The City God angrily said: “Wang Yao, you had sons and yet could not discipline them properly, bringing it about that your posterity was cut off. Who will come to make offerings to you?” After saying this, the City God ordered the ghost soldiers to drive Wang Yao off. Wang Yao could only wail and go away. The next day the temple master went to visit Wang Yao’s home, and only then learned that Wang Yao had been dead for more than a year.

A saying of old goes: “Confucius’s sons did not know cursing; Zengzi’s sons did not know quarreling.” These are all the result of habit becoming nature! It says again: “Raising sons and younger brothers is like raising orchid and fragrant grass: one must both accumulate learning to cultivate them, and accumulate good to nourish them.” A father must not dote excessively on his sons. Sons and younger brothers should be strictly disciplined from early youth; once grown, they will not have the regret of unworthy offspring. It says again: “If the household has several children, food and clothing should be distributed fairly; the precedence of elder and younger, high and low, must be strictly carried out; right and wrong, good and evil, good and bad, must be clearly distinguished. When sons and younger brothers are small, teach them fairness, and when grown there will be no disaster of contending over property; discipline them strictly from early youth, and when grown there will be no disaster of insubordination and arrogance; from childhood teach them to distinguish good from evil and right from wrong, and when grown there will be no disaster of becoming ruffians and bandits. Taken together with what has been said before, one will then know how to act.”
A daughter-in-law who is not filial and not respectful toward her parents-in-law.

A daughter-in-law serving her parents-in-law is like a son serving his parents: her attitude should be gentle and pleasant-spoken, with a soft voice and lowered tone; she should be concerned for her parents-in-law’s cold and warmth, illness and itch, and support them when they come and go. If she is in the least lacking in propriety toward her parents-in-law, it is unfilial; and this sin of unfiliality reaches the heavens and may even bring upon her the retribution of being struck dead by thunder and fire. Alas! The relation of daughter-in-law to parents-in-law is formed by her marriage to the son; while the relation of son to parents is the innate kinship of blood! From ancient times, is there such a principle that a son is unfilial to his parents, yet a daughter-in-law is filial to her parents-in-law? So whenever a daughter-in-law fails in propriety toward her parents-in-law, it is all caused by the son. So how could ghosts and spirits single out the daughter-in-law’s unfiliality to punish? I hope that all who are sons will ponder this deeply!

On the twenty-second day of the third month of the fifth year of the Chongzhen era of the Ming dynasty, the wife of Mao Jizong of Shanyang county in Huai’an, Lady Feng, was by nature utterly filial. Her mother-in-law was advanced in age and gravely ill, and Mao Jizong just happened to be transporting grain to the capital. Lady Feng, having no recourse, that night bathed and changed her clothes, prayed to Heaven to die in her mother-in-law’s place, and then took a knife and stabbed herself in the side, so that the tip of her liver protruded. At that moment she suddenly heard her son cry out; fearing it would wake her mother-in-law, she used a handkerchief to temporarily cover the wound, went into the room to soothe the child. Afterwards, she worried that a little liver might not suffice to cure her mother-in-law’s illness, so she prayed devoutly and then cut again. At that time the moon had not yet come out, but the sky suddenly became bright and clear, and the stars shone forth brilliantly, shining upon Lady Feng as brightly as broad daylight. She cut another piece of her liver, immediately cooked it into a soup, and gave it to her mother-in-law to eat. As soon as her mother-in-law put it in her mouth, she found it exceptionally sweet and asked her: “What is this? How is it so delicious?” Lady Feng pretended and said: “A neighbor caught a deer; this is deer liver.” Her mother-in-law then drank up all the soup. Strangely enough, her illness was cured. Because Lady Feng at the time was moved by utmost sincerity, her wound did not feel painful. But the bloodstains were hard to conceal, and were detected by her young sister-in-law. The whole family spread the news in astonishment, and only then did the mother-in-law learn that it was her daughter-in-law who had saved her. Moved to sobs and tears, she cherished her daughter-in-law all the more. At the time the scholars of the village decided to write up this deed and present it to the emperor, but they were troubled by the boundless extortion of the officials and could not get the matter up to the emperor’s knowledge. Fortunately there was a scholar of Huizhou, Jiang Tianyi, who wrote a book, The Collection of Startling Filialty That Moved Heaven, and so this deed was passed down.

In the Song dynasty, Jia Dan served as the military governor of Huazhou. At the time there was a common woman who served her mother-in-law unfilially. Because the mother-in-law was old and blind, the woman gave her filthy food to eat; the mother-in-law found the taste strange. When the son returned from outside, she pulled at the son and asked. The son, seeing that his wife had actually given filth to his mother to eat, raised his face to heaven and wept bitterly. Suddenly, a peal of thunder flashed, cut off the woman’s head, and joined a dog’s head onto her neck. When Jia Dan learned of this, he ordered the woman to be led out and paraded through the streets within his jurisdiction, to warn the unfilial.
